<hr>

# AF1204 - Guide on Group and Individual Project Assignments

This guide consolidates all essential information about the group and individual project assignments for this module. It includes grading criteria, submission requirements, technical instructions, and support resources to help you succeed.


## 1. Assessment Overview

This module is assessed via two project assignments. Both components require the use of Python, its packages (especially `marimo`), and tools in the GitHub ecosystem introduced during the module.

| Component | Weighting | Due Date | Submission Platform |
| :---- | :--- | :-------- | :--------- |
| **Group Project** | 50% | **Week 7:** `r groupProject_deadline` | Moodle (Written Report) & <br>GitHub (Code) |
| **Individual Project** | 50% | **Week 12:** `r indivProject_deadline` | Moodle (Video Report) & <br>GitHub (Code) |

---

## 2. Group Project Assignment (50%)

### Objective
Collaborate to create a single **interactive dashboard** using S&P 500 company financials and/or stock data.

### Group Formation
- Groups are **5 members** each.
- Sign-up deadline is `r groupFormation_deadline`.
    - Self-sign-up on Moodle
    - **Non-sign-ups** were manually allocated to **unfilled vacancies of self-formed groups** with less than 5 members

### Deliverables & Submission Requirements

**1. The Written Report (Submitted to Moodle)**

- **Length:** Maximum 1,500 words.
- **Content:** Describe how the group utilized coding/data skills (from the module or self-exploration) to prepare data, visualize it, and create the interactive dashboard.
- **Format Options:** You must submit the report in **one** of the following formats:
    - **(Option A)** An HTML file exported directly from a Marimo notebook.
    - **(Option B)** A PDF file produced via MS Word or similar software.
- **WARNING:** Do **NOT** submit a pdf file printed from a marimo-exported html file because certain visible contents of the exported file might not be printable to a pdf file
- **Further details:** See section 7.1

**2. Supporting Code (Made available on GitHub)**

- **Location:** The root directory of the main branch of your designated **Group Repository** (e.g., `project-group99`)
- **Requirement:** <span style="color:red;">Working Python code in a marimo notebook that generates the interactive dashboard described in your report</span>
- **Commit History:** You must <span style="color:red;">save work regularly</span>. The group’s independent work is evidenced by a consistent Git commit history from group members

---

## 3. Individual Project Assignment (50%)

### Objective
Create a **personal portfolio webpage** demonstrating your data literacy skills.

### Deliverables & Submission Requirements

**1. The Video Report (Submitted to Moodle)**

- **Length:** Maximum **3 minutes**
- **Format:** MP4 video file
- **Content:** A "showcase" of your portfolio webpage. The video must include:
    - Narration (voiceover explaining the work)
    - Screen recording of the device exploring the webpage
    - **Picture-in-Video:** Your face must be visible (e.g., a webcam bubble/window) throughout the presentation to verify identity
- **Focus:** Highlight specific features that demonstrate skills acquired from the module (Weeks 1-10) or self-exploration of closely related tools and techniques. Articulate your technical journey in a way suitable for potential employers
* **Further details:** See section 7.2

**2. Supporting <span style="color:red;">Webpage (Accessible at default URL)</span> and Code (Made available on GitHub)**

- **Webpage**
    - **Default URL:** In the format of `https://bayesug-ai.github.io/repoAF1204-[yourGitHubUsername]`, where `[yourGitHubUsername]` is the GitHub username indicated in the filename of the submitted video file: <span style="color:red;">`[StudentEmailAddress]_[StudentIDNumber]_[yourGitHubUsername].mp4`</span> (replacing the `[]` placeholders by your actual student email address, student ID number, and GitHub username)
    - **Requirement:** <span style="color:red;">Webpage can be successfully loaded and is working in every aspect as described and seen in the video</span>
- **Code**  
    - **Location:** The root directory of the main branch of your **personal forked module repository** (specifically the repo with `repoAF1204-[yourGitHubUsername]`)
    - **Requirement:** Working Python code in marimo notebook(s) that generates the portfolio webpage

---

## 4. Assessment & Grading Criteria

The written report (Group) and video report (Individual) are the primary documents read/watched for grading. However, lecturers may review the supporting Python code on GitHub to assess the independence and validity of the work.

Marks are awarded based on the skills demonstrated in the written / video report. The following tables summarise the requirements for each mark range.

| **Group Project** Mark Range &nbsp; | Required Competencies |
|:-----|:-----------------|
| 40–60 | Coding and data skills covered in Week 1 to 4. |
| 61–75 | All of the above, plus basic additional skills from self-exploration of closely related tools and techniques for any week(s). |
| 76+ | All of the above, plus enhanced additional skills from self-exploration of closely related tools and techniques for any week(s). |

| **Indiv. Project** Mark Range | Required Competencies |
|:-----|:-----------------|
| 40–60 | Coding and data skills covered in Week 1 to 4. |
| 61–75 | All of the above, plus **at least one** of:  <br>(i) additional skills from self-exploration of closely related tools and techniques for any week(s); <br>(ii) skills covered in Week 6 and 10. |
| 76+ | All of the above, plus skills covered in Week 7 to 9 AND additional skills from self-exploration of closely related tools and techniques for any week(s). |

_**Note**: Within each mark range, students who **more convincingly demonstrate higher competence** in their written/video report will earn marks **closer to the upper end** of that range._

---

## 5. Academic Integrity & AI Policy

- **Independent Work:** Submissions must be your own (or your group's own).
- **AI Usage:** You are **encouraged** to use AI tools (e.g., GitHub Copilot) as learning partners. However, you must:
    - Understand the AI-suggested solutions.
    - Exercise judgment to accept/reject/revise suggestions.
    - Be able to explain or reproduce the work independently if asked.
- **Contract Cheating:** Strictly prohibited. Never use third parties to produce work for you.
- **Evidence:** "Version control history" (commit logs) will be reviewed as part of integrity verification. A lack of meaningful commit history (for example, a project appearing in a single upload) may be considered supporting evidence that the work was not completed incrementally by the student. Students must ensure their work leaves an appropriate **digital trail** within the GitHub environment.

---

## 6. How to Create Your Video Report (Step-by-Step)

You need to record your screen, your voice, and your face simultaneously. The resulting file must be an **MP4**.

### Test your equipment:
- Microphone: Ensure clear audio capture
- Webcam: Position so your face is well-lit and visible
- Screen resolution: Set to 1920x1080 if possible for best quality



### Option A: Using Zoom (Recommended for University Accounts)


1.  **Open Zoom** and start a **"New Meeting"** (with just yourself in it).
2.  **Turn on your Camera** so your face is visible in the meeting window.
3.  Click the **"Share Screen"** button at the bottom.
4.  Select the specific window (browser) showing your Portfolio Webpage and click **Share**.
    - *Note: By default, Zoom places your video feed in a floating window on top of the shared screen.*
5.  Hover over the meeting controls (usually at the top of the screen), click **"More" (...)**, and select **"Record on this Computer"**.
6.  **Start presenting!** Navigate through your portfolio while narrating. Keep an eye on the time (Max 3 mins).
7.  When finished, click **"Stop Recording"** in the controls.
8.  Click **"End Meeting for All"**.
9.  Zoom will automatically convert the recording. Once finished, it will open the folder containing your file (usually named `zoom_0.mp4`). **Rename this file** before uploading to Moodle.

### Option B: Using Loom (Easiest Free Alternative)
*Loom is a browser-based tool specifically designed for screen+cam recording. It is very beginner-friendly.*

1.  Go to [loom.com](https://loom.com) and sign up for a free account.
2.  Install the **Loom Chrome Extension** (or desktop app).
3.  Open your Portfolio Webpage in your browser.
4.  Click the Loom icon. Ensure the settings are:
    - **Screen and Camera** (selected).
    - **Microphone audio** (on).
5.  You will see a circular "bubble" with your face in the corner. You can move this bubble so it doesn't block important content.
6.  Click **"Start Recording"**.
7.  Present your work. When done, click the **Stop** button (square).
8.  Loom will open your video in a browser. Click the **Download** button to save the **MP4 file** to your computer.
9.  Upload this MP4 file to Moodle.

## 7. Quick Reference Checklist

### 7.1 Group Project Checklist

- Accept the GitHub Classroom invitation for your group repo: `r invitation_group_repo`
- Coordinate with your group and divide tasks
- Build a single **interactive** dashboard using S&P 500 data, based on the Week 4 marimo notebook templates and coding techniques from Week 1-4
- **Commit** your individual contributions **regularly** to the group repo
- Check all links, visualisations, and interactive elements in the **dashboard notebook** to ensure they function correctly
    - Confirm the notebook can be **run as a web app** (see instructions in the Week 4 marimo notebook)
- Prepare the written report (&le; 1,500 words) in the correct format (HTML exported from marimo, or PDF printed from Word)
- The beginning of the report should show the **project group number**, the **<span style="color:red;">filename of the interactive dashboard notebook</span>** in the **main** branch of your group repo, and **each <span style="color:red;">active</span> group member's student ID and school email address**. (Exclude **inactive** members, who are those with insignificant or nocontribution.)
    - _Note:_ Active group members will receive the same mark for the group project. Inactive members will receive a zero mark for the group project.
- Name the file in the format of `group[XX]_Project.html` or `group[XX]_Project.pdf` (replacing the `[XX]` placeholder by the actual group number, e.g., `99`)
- Ensure the **notebook** that generated the interactive dashboard is in The root directory of the main branch of the group GitHub repo (e.g., `project-group99`)
- Submit the report on **Moodle** by `r groupProject_deadline`

### 7.2 Individual Project Checklist

- Build a personal portfolio webpage based on the Week 4 marimo notebook templates 
    - Ensure the webpage is working fully in every aspect according to your design and **reachable at its default URL** (in the format of `https://bayesug-ai.github.io/repoAF1204-[yourGitHubUsername]`)
    - <span style="color:red;">Ensure the URL of the webpage can be clearly seen in the screen recorded in the submitted video file</span>
- **Commit** your work in progress **regularly** to your personal forked repo
- Record a 3-minute **MP4** video with **narration**, **screen recording**, and **picture-in-picture** (PiP) webcam (e.g., using Zoom or Loom)
- Verify the MP4 file: audio, screen <span style="color:red;">(with visible webpage URL)</span>, and PiP webcam all present; duration ≤ 3 minutes
- Name the file in the format of `[StudentEmailAddress]_[StudentIDNumber]_[yourGitHubUsername].mp4` (replacing the `[]` placeholders by your actual student email address, student ID number, and GitHub username)
- Ensure the **notebook** that generated the webpage is in The root directory of the main branch of your personal forked GitHub repo (with `repoAF1204-`) 
- <span style="color:red;">Ensure the **<span style="color:red;">webpage</span>** <span style="color:red;">can be successfully loaded at its default URL (in the format of `https://bayesug-ai.github.io/repoAF1204-[yourGitHubUsername]`)</span>
- Submit the MP4 video on **Moodle** `r indivProject_deadline`

## 9. FAQs

### 9.0 Generally Applicable FAQs

- _**I've exceeded the monthly usage budget for Codespaces. Is there an alternative way for me to continue my work on the assignmennt?**_

    - Please read **all relevant FAQs** in section 9  of the Guide **concerning running out of credits**.


- _**I have used up the monthly free credit allowance on GitHub but I am not comfortable providing my bank details to GitHub for purchasing credits. What alternatives do I have?**_
    - FWIW, I ran into a similar situation and had provided my Revolut card details to pay for a subscription. I paid for a pay-as-you-go subscription and added only as much an amount as necessary in my Revolut account to allow payment to GitHub. Since that incident, I managed my usage very carefully and had not run into the same situation again. I also reverted the budget limit back to zero so that GitHub would stop my usage once I hit the monthly allowance (you must raise the budget limit beyond 0 to allow usage once the monthly allowance is reached, and to raise the limit, you must provide a payment method). But the zero budget limit has not been binding since I learned to manage my allowance well. 
    - Additionally, you can explore molab and lightning.ai as alternative code development environments. See relevant entries in section 9 FAQs of the [Guide](`r guide_Indiv_URL`). In the Week 10 session, I also mentioned the alternative of a locally installed environment. Watch the part of the lecture recording concerning VS Code. However, this requires a user to have much higher technical background to be able to do it successfully.
    - The alternative environments allow you to develop the marimo notebook for generating the ultimate webpage. Successfully running the marimo notebook as a web app using the `mairmo run` command is necessary (not sufficient) for the webpage to work when exported as html-wasm. Eventually, you must upload the developed marimo notebook back to your GitHub repo, fire up a Codespace to export the notebook in html-wasm to the `docs` folder, commit the changes back to the GitHub repo, go through the steps to enable the default URL of the webpage, and verify whether it could be successfully loaded. 


- _**I have uncommitted changes in a Codespace created from my repo. Because the credit allowance for this month has been used up, I can no longer reactivate the Codespace to get back the files with the uncommitted changes. The Codespace will be auto-deleted in a few days. What should I do?**_
    - This situation highlights the importance of committing changes regularly and ensuring all changes have been committed before you let a Codespace sleep. If you had, all the changed files are now in your branch of the group project repo. 
    - The only potential rescue I could think of is an export option on the Codespaces dashboard page that might be relevant -- though I am not 100% sure it does serve your purpose here. Anyway, give it a try.
    - ![](img/ExportOption.jpeg){width=50%}


- _**My GitHub Codespace usage limit has run out, and my account indicates it won't reset until the next calendar month begins. Is there an alternative method or setup you recommend that lets me continue using GitHub Codespaces to work on the module assignments?**_
    - There's not much you can do when it gets to this stage. All the free GitHub services go under a total credit allowance. When it is exhausted, you have to wait until the allowance is replenished in the next monthly cycle. 
        - Given the total credit allowance, you cannot use Codespaces as virtual computers beyond certain hours. The total number of hours available is also affected by the sizes of the Codespaces you have created and kept. The storage usage is on a storage-hour basis in terms of how it consumes the credit allowance. Deleting unused Codespaces can stop bleeding but it won't change the fact that previously credits were wasted on keeping unused Codespaces.
    - Going forward, please consider keeping an eye on the usage from time to time and having a read of the documentation on the pricing for different things: Codespaces storage cost, Copilot, etc. See those pages in the screenshots attached below. I guess some of your slept Codespaces might have taken up a portion of your storage allowance. It is a good practice to actively delete unused Codespaces and refrain from creating new ones unless absolutely necessary.  
    - Not sure relevant in this particular case but have you followed [the advice to apply for additional Education benefits from GitHub](`r github_ecosystem_section`)?
        - _Follow the instructions on [this page](`r github_eduBenefits_URL`) to apply for **GitHub Education benefits for verified students**:_
            - _Verified students can receive Copilot Pro for free, 180 monthly Codespaces hours for cloud coding, unlimited private repositories with GitHub Pro or Team, and dozens of premium tools in the GitHub Student Developer Pack._
            - (_Note_: It can take over five working days to obtain the approval for the additional benefits even if all the required documents are submitted properly.)
    - A potential short-term workaround: 
        - Try whether you are able to use a personal email address to register for another GitHub account.
        - If you have a second GitHub account, you can invite the second you as a collaborator to your branch of the group repo. Click `Accept` from the collaboration invitation email. Start a Codespace from the repo in a browser where the second you has logged in GitHub by default. I believe the usage should then count under the second you. 
    - Worst comes to worst, you might want to consider the paid subscription option. 
    - You can also try using **molab** as an alternative platform but the environment is quite different, and we have not tested the module notebooks on that platform.
        - [Announcing molab | marimo](https://marimo.io/blog/announcing-molab): 
            - https://molab.marimo.io/
    - ![](img/GitHubBilling1.png){width=100%}
    - ![](img/GitHubBilling2.png){width=100%}
    - ![](img/GitHubBilling3.png){width=100%}


- _**I can't talk to the github copilot AI anymore. It says I have to upgrade to the plus version. What should I do?**_
    1. Don't waste AI resources. If an AI cannot fix an issue within 3 iterations, give up the change and try something else. Please also read other relevant FAQs in section 9 of this Guide.
    2. Use cheaper models for simpler tasks to conserve credits. Those with &times;3 mean more powerful models consuming 3 times the credits of a regular model (&times;1). There should be cheaper or even free models (&times;0.25 and &times;0).
    3. Try alternative AI providers described in this Moodle section: `r alt_AIs_section`
    4. Going forward, keep up with your learning on a weekly basis so that you consume the monthly credit allowance for AI gradually to prevent hitting the cap like this. 
    5. If you could afford (and have used up the limited free allowances elsewhere too), pay for one-month subscription of GitHub Copilot (if they have this option)


- _**We already learned how to use GitHub Codespaces. Why is it useful to learn to use Lightning.ai as an alternative cloud computing platform for working on the module assignments?**_
    - 4-core CPU sessions on _Lightning.ai_ are entirely free up to the first 4 hours of a session. If you remember to put a Studio (the equivalent of a GitHub Codespace) into sleep at the end of a 4-hour session and then put it back on to refresh the free status, effectively you have free use of 4-core CPU sessions “as long as you want”. 
        - In that sense, you will never run out of credits on _Lightning.ai_ and can reserve the monthly 15 free credits on this platform for up to 75 hours of GPU usage -- which otherwise is only available to owners of [a machine of over £1,200](`r GPU_machine`).


- _**Whenever I try to commit changes and sync my work, the error message in the screenshot below pops up. What should I do?**_ ![](img/File_conflicts_redacted.png){width=100%}
    - The situation could be a consequence of changing the same file through different channels without always committing back to the repo immediately. For example, at 9:00 on a day you changed a file in the Codespace created from a repo without committing the change back to the repo. At 14:00, you went to the GitHub repo page and directly edited the same file. At 18:00, you worked with the Codespace again and decided to sync your changes in that file back to the repo. At that point, the file in the repo was changed at 14:00, whereas the same file in the Codespace was changed at 18:00. The version controlling system (Git) was not sure which version you really want to keep and therefore would require you to take actions to clearly indicate how you would like the changes to be integrated together. Usually, this would require an interaction with the Git system using the command line interface (cli) to handle properly. The Git Log contains hints on the git commands for consideration. Following through this path requires some technical knowledge on your side. 
    - The exact cause of your case might be different but this is obviously a file conflict situation. A tedious but easy-to-follow approach to resolving the issue is to download all the latest versions of the changed files from the Codespace to your device and then directly upload them back to the GitHub repo. 
        - In the Explorer panel, you can right-click on each file in concern and select Download from the pop-up dropdown menu to download it to your own pc. 
        - Open your GitHub repo page, click on the 'Add file' button next to the green 'Code' button and select 'Upload files'. 
    - When you upload a copy of the same filename to the repo, you give the permission to replace the existing copy. When this is done, all your files in the repo is up-to-date. From thereon, create a new Codespace to continue your work (and delete the old Codespace that could not be synced) and maintain a good practice of always committing changed files back to the repo at the end of each work session. 


- _**I accidentally deleted my code. When I try to do it from the start, it keeps giving me this `redefined variable` error (see the screenshot). What should I do?**_ ![](img/RedefinedVariableError.jpg){width=100%}
    - First of all, make sure there is not another cell in which you also have the `import micropip` statement because this would redefine the object `micropip` &mdash; a <span style="color:red;">**marimo don't**</span> (see a [Week 11 slide](`r Week11_slides_URL`)) &mdash; and cause the error. If there is, you can simply delete the `import micropip` statement in the other cell to fix the issue.
    - If the above had been confirmed but the error persisted, maybe marimo got confused **due to some cache in the sandbox created**. You can try the below to see whether it can fix the issue:
        - Save your notebook with a new filename.
        - Alternatively, first create a new marimo notebook, next use `Ctrl-A` to select all cells in the old notebook and  `Ctrl-C` to copy them. Then go to the newly created notebook and use `Ctrl-V` to paste the copied cells into the new notebook. Save the changes in the new notebook. 
        - The kernel of the new notebook should not have been selected yet. Set the kernel to `marimo sandbox`, which would then be rebuilt. 
        - The `redefined variable` error might go away after the sandbox is rebuilt. 


- _**I already know how to use Streamlit to create a web app. May I use it instead of the required marimo notebook to finish the module assignments?**_
    - If a module teaches Chinese Medicine, students should not be allowed to pass the module by proving that they can cure patients with Western Medicine. Similarly, C++ code cannot be used for passing a module teaching Javascript. 
    - FWIW, Gemini has the following opinions on whether Streamlit is better than marimo:  
        - While Streamlit is more popular and excels at rapid, linear app development, marimo offers superior performance through reactive execution and a more flexible development workflow.
        - **Key Performance Differences**
            - Execution Model: Streamlit reruns your entire script from top to bottom on every interaction, which can lead to lag in larger apps. Marimo uses a directed acyclic graph (DAG) to rerun only the cells that depend on a changed variable, making it significantly faster.
            - **State Management**: Streamlit requires explicit use of `st.session_state` to persist data across reruns. Marimo manages state naturally through its reactive variables, reducing boilerplate code.
        - **Workflow and Versatility**
            - **Notebook-First**: Marimo is a reactive notebook that can be deployed as an app, meaning you don't have to rewrite code from a prototype (like Jupyter) into a separate app framework.
            - **Deployment Options**: Marimo files can be run as web apps, executed as standard Python scripts, or even exported to WASM for serverless browser execution.
            - **SQL Integration**: Marimo has native SQL support, allowing you to query dataframes directly with SQL cells and have the results flow back into Python. 


- _**Since I ran out of the credit allowance for using Codespaces, I developed my code on a local host (http://localhost:2721/). This would not cause any issue, would it?**_
    - I trust you can appreciate that there's not an easy way to verify students' work in their personal device; we have no access to your localhost. 
    - Your assignment will be verified against files on your repo that are dated before the submission deadline (for late submissions, up to two days after the submission deadline). 
    - Running out of credits to use a Codespace is not an excuse not to upload the marimo notebook developed in your local device back to your repo on a **daily basis**.

### 9.1 Group Project FAQs

- _**What needs to be included in the Interactive Dashboard and the written group project report in order to achieve a high grade?**_
    - Let me use a metaphor to explain the consideration. In the free skate segment of an ice-skating athlete’s program, the athlete selects movements to showcase their skills. However, neither a difficult movement that is poorly executed nor a trivial movement is likely to impress the panel of judges. Instead, the program must be built around elements that are among the most challenging the athlete can perform while still being executed with confidence and consistency.
    - Returning to the context of the group project assignment, you should similarly select coding skills—whether learned in this module or through self-directed exploration of related tools and techniques—to showcase what you have learned. Using the interactive dashboard required by the assignment and within the approximately 1,500-word limit of the written group project report, **explain where** (for example, the Week 2 marimo notebook) **and, where relevant, how** (for example, through experimentation inspired by a blog post or YouTube video) **you learned these techniques**. You should place particular **emphasis on those skills that you found most challenging**.
    - Please also refer to details in the document [Guide on Group and Individual Project Assignments](`r guide_Group_URL`) (especially, Section 4): 


- _**I have created my own branch. Should I edit and extend the `Wk04w_Dashboard.py` file there directly, or creating a new file instead, to develop it into the final one to be merged back to the main branch later?**_
    - In your own branch, save the file as another copy with a different name (hamburger button, File | Save as). When it has been fully developed and is ready to be merged back to the main branch, do it as a “merge pull request” as shown in a video provided on Moodle. Because the name of that file is unique in both branches, the “merge pull request” process should be straightforward. 


- _**By collaboration in the group project assignment, do you mean simply separating the tasks among the group members like one for preparing the data, one for preparing the interactive features, one for writing up the report, etc?**_
    - One important element of group work is **mutual monitoring**. The very reason why the University and the School wanted modules to incorporate group assignment is to give students the opportunities to experience the **challenges coming from group dynamics** and experiment with alternatives to overcome them. Because all the members are **jointly responsible for the group work outcome**, one should not assume things would necessarily work out smoothly without checking in with each other on progress from time to time to achieve good time management.
    - Another important element of group work is **mutual learning**. Group assignments are not just about producing a final deliverable efficiently; they are also designed to help you learn from one another. Each member may bring different strengths, perspectives, and skills, and engaging with these differences can deepen everyone’s understanding of the subject. This means **discussing ideas together, explaining your approaches, asking questions, and giving constructive feedback** &mdash; not just working in isolated parts.
    - In practice, effective collaboration usually involves a balance: **some division of tasks** for efficiency, combined with **regular communication, shared decision-making, and collective review of the work**. This helps ensure consistency, improves overall quality, and allows all members to contribute meaningfully to—and learn from—the entire project, not just their individual section.
    - Please also see what could happen if one's contribution was disputed by other group members: 
        - _Based on the evidence you provided for the purpose of "proving your significant contributions", I decided to adjust your mark to XX to reflect your contribution to the group work. Please refer to the attached documents for the basis of the decision._
        - _In my email on February 18, I made clear that students "are expected to save their work in progress back to the Group repo from time to time ... You will be in a vulnerable position if your group mates dispute your contributions, and you cannot provide clear evidence to the contrary." The importance of a commit history was also reiterated multiple times in the Guide on Group and Individual Project Assignments._
        - _You put yourself in a vulnerable position by only working on the report. You also gave up an opportunity to deepen the understanding of the skills you should have learned from the module._ 
        - _While the outcome of the review may not be what you hoped for, I hope this experience helps you improve in the future._


- _**I am not good at groupwork. What changes should I make to become better in working with strangers in groups? Can you suggest some YouTube videos for me to understand the topic better?**_
    - We are in the AI age! I passed your questions to Gemini. It gave the following reply: 
        - Working with strangers in a group project can definitely be a challenging experience, but making a few intentional changes to how you approach teamwork can make a massive difference. 
        - Based on expert advice from the Beedie School of Business, here are some actionable changes you can make to become a better teammate when working with people you don't know:
        * **Build Trust Early:** Before diving straight into the workload, try organizing a casual hangout with your group. Taking this small step helps build mutual respect and trust right from the beginning, which eases tension [[01:12](`r paste0(groupwork_youtube, "&t=72")`)].
        * **Establish a "Group Contract":** Once you sit down to work, collaborate to create a simple agreement that outlines basic expectations, expected response times, and general ground rules. It is also highly recommended to set an ongoing, predictable meeting time so everyone can schedule around it [[01:26](`r paste0(groupwork_youtube, "&t=86")`)].
        * **Divide Tasks by Strengths:** Don't just assign work randomly. Take a few minutes to figure out what each person excels at or enjoys doing. For example, assign the report editing to a strong writer, and the slide deck to someone with an eye for design [[01:52](`r paste0(groupwork_youtube, "&t=112")`)].
        * **Avoid Over-Contributing:** When working with strangers, it can be tempting to take on the majority of the project yourself to ensure it gets done correctly. However, this often causes others to step back and contribute less. You have to give your team members the space and opportunity to do their share [[02:22](`r paste0(groupwork_youtube, "&t=142")`)].
        * **Set Mini-Milestones:** Long group projects can feel grueling. Break the larger objective down into smaller, manageable milestones and celebrate or reward yourselves when you hit them to keep motivation high [[02:10](`r paste0(groupwork_youtube, "&t=130")`)].
        * **Use Targeted Mini-Meetings:** You don't always need the entire group present to get work done. If two people are collaborating on a specific section, encourage them to meet up separately to accomplish their tasks more efficiently [[02:35](`r paste0(groupwork_youtube, "&t=155")`)].
        * **Handle Conflict Constructively:** If a group member isn't delivering, don't immediately point fingers. Consider if there is a flaw in the group dynamic causing the bottleneck, and when you address it, use "we" language to focus on the issue rather than attacking the person [[03:04](`r paste0(groupwork_youtube, "&t=184")`)].
        * **Document Contributions:** Keep clear records of who communicates what and who contributes which parts of the project. A great trick is to assign a specific text color to each person in your shared documents so their work is clearly identifiable [[02:46](`r paste0(groupwork_youtube, "&t=166")`)].
        * **Recommended YouTube Video to Help You Further:** **[How to Deal With Difficult Group Project Members](`r groupwork_youtube`)** by *SFU Beedie School of Business* – This video humorously breaks down the different "types" of difficult team members (like procrastinators, the "dead weights," and self-appointed bosses) and offers excellent practical steps on how to structure a group project from the start so that you can work seamlessly with anyone.
